strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: reducing communication in DiLoCo-style training, which is important for distributed/decentralized LLM pre-training.

The core empirical finding—that Muon's orthogonalized updates are more compressible than AdamW's, enabling 2-bit quantization with error feedback at 8x less communication with no performance loss—is a clean, interesting, and potentially useful observation.

Reasonably thorough ablation across compression schemes (top-k, quantization, DCT top-k, random-k) and with/without error feedback, including extensive hyperparameter sweep documentation in the appendix, which aids reproducibility.
Clear algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) that explicitly highlights the modifications made to standard DiLoCo, making the method easy to understand and reimplement.
Correct and useful memory-complexity accounting (Table 1) showing MuLoCo+EF matches DiLoCo's memory footprint while communicating far less.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted at a single, small model scale (220M parameters, K=8 workers, H=30), with no scaling experiments to larger models or worker counts; given DiLoCo's known scale-dependent behavior (cited scaling-law work), it is unclear whether the 2-bit MuLoCo result holds at larger scales, which are the primary practical setting motivating this line of work.

No wall-clock time or realistic network-bandwidth analysis is provided; the paper explicitly states it does not account for wall-clock time, yet communication efficiency claims are fundamentally about wall-clock/bandwidth benefits, weakening the practical significance claim.

Single-seed runs appear to be used throughout (no reported variance, error bars, or multiple seeds), making it hard to assess whether the reported small margins (e.g., MuLoCo 2-bit vs no-compression) are statistically meaningful or within run-to-run noise.

The mechanistic explanation for why Muon's updates compress better is only qualitative/hypothesized ('distinctly different update structure') without deeper analysis (e.g., spectral/singular value analysis of the delta, or theoretical grounding) connecting orthogonalization to quantization/sparsification robustness.

The comparison baseline for AdamW-DiLoCo compression is somewhat weaker than expected from prior work (e.g., Streaming DiLoCo shows more graceful degradation under compression for AdamW-DiLoCo), and the paper does not fully reconcile or discuss why quantization degrades AdamW-DiLoCo so severely at 2 bits without deeper diagnosis.

Data-parallel comparisons in Fig. 3 do not control for total optimizer/communication cost equivalently across Muon vs AdamW baselines in terms of realistic deployment (e.g., different learning-rate schedules/optimal HPs may bias comparisons among baselines).

The writing has some presentation issues, including typos/formatting errors (e.g., 'Litterature Review', inconsistent figure captions in Figs. 5-6 mislabeled as 'training curves' for training loss without axis label fixes, some redundant phrasing), which slightly reduce clarity.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines known components (DiLoCo + Muon + standard compression + error feedback) rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithmic techniques; the main contribution is an empirical observation rather than a new method or theoretical insight.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically relevant gap: the interaction between the DiLoCo inner optimizer choice (Muon vs AdamW), error-feedback accumulation, and aggressive compression (top-k, quantization, DCT-based, random-k) has not been jointly studied for LLM pre-training.

The empirical study is reasonably comprehensive: it sweeps multiple compression schemes and strengths, ablates error feedback for each, and reports memory complexity trade-offs (Table 1) alongside communication savings.

The central empirical finding -- that Muon's orthogonalized update structure is markedly more resilient to 2-bit quantization with error feedback than AdamW's update, enabling an 8x communication reduction while matching or beating the AdamW-DiLoCo baseline -- is a clean, useful, and actionable result for practitioners.
Reasonable transparency about hyperparameter tuning procedure and values (Appendix E, Tables 2-5), and inclusion of full per-scheme training curves (Figs 5-6) aids reproducibility.

Ablations against data-parallel baselines (Fig 3) and consideration of multiple compression families (top-k, quantization, DCT top-k, random-k) show an attempt at thoroughness rather than cherry-picking a single compression method.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted at a single, small model scale (220M parameters) and a single distributed configuration (K=8 workers, H=30 local steps). Since DiLoCo's practical motivation is training much larger models over slow networks, it is unclear whether the compressibility advantage of Muon persists at larger scale, larger K, or larger H -- and the paper does not discuss this generalization risk.

No wall-clock or compute-time comparison is provided. Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization adds nontrivial per-step compute overhead relative to AdamW; the paper's headline comparison (Fig. 1) only tracks bits communicated versus loss, which can overstate the practical benefit if compute time is the actual bottleneck in some deployment settings.

The experiments appear to be single-seed (no error bars, variance, or repeated runs are reported anywhere in the main text or appendix), so it is difficult to assess whether the reported gaps (e.g., MuLoCo vs DiLoCo at 2-bit quantization) are statistically robust or within run-to-run noise, especially given the moderate size of the loss differences shown in Fig. 2.

The contribution is primarily an empirical recombination of existing components (Muon, error-feedback accumulators, standard quantization/top-k compressors) rather than a new algorithm or theoretical insight; the paper offers only an informal hypothesis ('Muon's update is qualitatively different, so it may compress differently') without any analysis of why Muon's orthogonalized deltas are more quantization-friendly.

The cross-scheme narrative is inconsistent: DCT-based top-k sometimes helps DiLoCo more than MuLoCo (Appendix C), and random-k compression catastrophically fails for both, but the paper does not analyze or explain these discrepancies, weakening the paper's central claim that Muon is uniformly a better DiLoCo inner optimizer for compression.

Hyperparameters were tuned in the no-compression regime (with the exception of the error-feedback beta) and then reused for all compressed configurations; this could differentially disadvantage certain compression/optimizer combinations and makes the head-to-head comparisons less rigorous.

No comparison against other existing communication-efficient distributed optimizers/compressors directly designed for this setting (e.g., PowerSGD, Dion, QSGD, CocktailSGD) is included, despite several being cited as related work; this limits the ability to contextualize how large the reported gains actually are relative to the state of the art.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: reducing DiLoCo's communication overhead while maintaining performance, with a clean and simple modification (swapping AdamW for Muon as inner optimizer) that is easy to adopt.

The central empirical finding is compelling and well illustrated (Fig. 1): MuLoCo with 2-bit quantization + error feedback matches or beats vanilla DiLoCo while using ~8x less communication and identical memory complexity, which is a clear practical win.

Systematic ablation design across two inner optimizers (AdamW, Muon), two compression families (top-k sparsification, quantization), and presence/absence of error feedback, isolating the individual and combined effects of each factor (Fig. 2).

Reasonably strong reproducibility support: detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1) highlighting exactly what was changed relative to standard DiLoCo, extensive hyperparameter tables (Tables 2-5), and reported sweep grids (Table 3) with sweep result plots in the appendix.
Useful extended experiments in the appendix (DCT top-k, random-k, per-configuration training curves) that go beyond the main results and help sanity-check robustness of the top-line claims.
The memory complexity comparison (Table 1) is a nice, concrete way to communicate why MuLoCo's savings are not just about bits communicated but also about accumulator overhead versus DiLoCo+EF.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted at a single small scale (220M parameters, K=8 workers, H=30 local steps); there is no scaling study (varying model size, worker count, or H) to establish whether the compressibility advantage of Muon persists or grows/shrinks at larger scale, which is important given the paper's stated motivation of training frontier-scale LLMs.

No wall-clock time or FLOPs comparison is provided; Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization introduces nontrivial compute overhead per step that is not accounted for, so the practical 'speedup' claim is only in terms of communicated bits, not actual training time savings.

Results appear to be based on single training runs (no reported seeds, error bars, or variance estimates), which is a concern given that the reported final-loss differences between conditions (e.g., in Fig. 2) are sometimes small relative to visible noise in the training curves.

The explanation for why Muon's orthogonalized updates compress better is largely empirical/post-hoc; no theoretical or spectral analysis of why orthogonalized deltas are more quantization/sparsification friendly is offered, leaving the core mechanism underexplored despite being central to the paper's narrative.

Comparisons to other recent communication-efficient optimizers/compression schemes tailored for LLM pretraining (e.g., DeMo, Dion, PowerSGD) are limited to a partial DCT top-k comparison in the appendix; a more direct comparison against these closely related baselines would strengthen the significance claims.

The random-k sparsification results show catastrophic degradation (Fig. 4, right) but this negative result is not analyzed or discussed in the main text, leaving an interesting but unexplained finding.

The main paper is quite short and the analysis in Sections 5.1-5.2 is largely descriptive of the figures rather than providing deeper insight into mechanisms (e.g., what actually differs in the spectral/structural properties of AdamW vs. Muon deltas that drives compressibility).

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical study: extensive hyperparameter sweeps (over 2,200 runs) across 5+ model scales (150M-3.1B) and 5 worker counts for four optimizer/framework combinations (DP AdamW, DP Muon, DiLoCo, MuLoCo), providing a level of rigor rarely seen in distributed optimization papers.

The core empirical finding is consistent, robust, and practically important: swapping AdamW for Muon as DiLoCo's inner optimizer improves worker scaling, critical batch size, and wall-clock time across many communication-efficient settings (long H, quantization, sparsification, streaming/partitioned communication).

Good mechanistic investigation combining several complementary empirical diagnostics (pseudogradient cosine similarity to K=1 baseline, spectral/interference-gap analysis, per-step alignment and Frobenius norm stability) that converge on a coherent story for why Muon's orthonormalized updates yield better-preserved pseudogradients under averaging.

A clean theoretical result (Proposition 4.2 and corollaries) formally relates the pseudogradient's nuclear norm to per-step cosine alignment and step magnitude, giving a principled account of why orthonormalized (Muon) steps stabilize the pseudogradient spectrum relative to AdamW's more variable step norms.

Practically relevant systems-level analysis: realistic modeling of quantized communication with all-to-all reduce-scatter + ring all-gather, wall-clock timing under different bandwidth regimes, and memory complexity comparisons, which ground the method in real deployment considerations rather than idealized FLOP counts alone.

Scaling-law fitting to 15B with reasonably careful methodology (multiple functional forms, held-out validation, robust Huber loss fitting) with an honest discussion of extrapolation uncertainty and limitations.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution, while correct, is largely a norm-decomposition identity (nuclear norm as alignment × Frobenius norm summed over steps) rather than a predictive or causal theory; the paper explicitly acknowledges it does not establish a direct causal link between the interference-gap findings and the observed performance gains, leaving the central 'why' still somewhat empirically conjectural.

The largest-scale (15B) experiments are single runs per method with no hyperparameter sweep and reliance on extrapolated (and admittedly imperfect, e.g., a previously-undetected local minimum in K=1 MuLoCo's batch size) hyperparameters, so the headline scale-validation claims rest on limited statistical evidence; no seeds/repeats or confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper to assess run-to-run variance.

Some 15B results are more mixed than the narrative suggests: MuLoCo K=16 actually has a *higher* (worse) evaluation loss than DiLoCo K=16 and DP AdamW, and its downstream mean accuracy advantage over DiLoCo K=16 is marginal (65.94% vs 65.68%), which is a weaker validation of the 'matches DP AdamW' claim than implied in the abstract/contributions list.

The manuscript contains an evident editing/completeness error: the Limitations section ends mid-sentence ('Finally, we did not evaluate the perfor'), suggesting the submission was not fully proofread or finalized, which raises minor concerns about overall care in presentation.

The extensive hyperparameter tuning protocol, while thorough, involves many manual choices and heuristics (e.g., reusing 416M-tuned outer optimizer HPs at all scales, rescaling weight decay via an external heuristic, rounding batch sizes to nearest power of 2) that add complexity and could affect reproducibility if implementation details are not fully released.

The wall-clock and bandwidth analyses (Figures 9, 14, 19) are 'idealized' estimates combining separately measured component timings rather than fully end-to-end wall-clock experiments at the largest scales, which is reasonable but somewhat weakens the practical validation of the claimed wall-clock benefits at 15B.

Coverage is limited to dense transformers under a fixed 20 TPP Chinchilla-style regime; generalization to MoE/other architectures or non-compute-optimal token budgets (acknowledged by the authors) remains unverified, limiting the generality of the scaling claims.

strengths: Extremely extensive empirical study (>2,200 pretraining runs across 150M-15B scale, 4 optimizers, K in {1,2,4,8,16}) with careful per-scale hyperparameter tuning, which is rare and valuable for a distributed-optimization paper.

The core empirical finding that MuLoCo's relative advantage over DiLoCo grows with worker count K, and that this cannot be explained solely by Muon's DP superiority over AdamW, is an interesting and non-obvious result.

Good practical coverage of real deployment concerns: long synchronization intervals, quantization/sparsification with and without error feedback, partitioned (streaming) communication, and measured (not just theoretical) wall-clock/system-level overhead.
The critical-batch-size analysis and its translation into a time-to-loss efficiency metric is a nice practical contribution showing a genuine systems-relevant benefit of MuLoCo at K=1.

An attempt at theoretical grounding (nuclear-norm decomposition in terms of per-step alignment and Frobenius norm) that at least provides a formal vocabulary for the empirical spectrum-collapse/interference-gap observations.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Prop. 4.2 and corollaries) is essentially an algebraic identity for the nuclear norm and does not itself explain *why* Muon's steps end up more aligned or why the interference gap shrinks with K; the causal story is still argued largely by appeal to empirical plots (Figs. 2-5), so the 'theory' section over-claims relative to what is actually proven.

No error bars, repeated seeds, or variance estimates are reported anywhere despite the paper making fine-grained quantitative claims (e.g., sub-percent MFU differences, <0.1% loss differences in Table 3, ordering of methods within 1-2% loss in Fig. 11); at 15B scale in particular only a single un-swept run per method is used to support the flagship scaling claims.

The headline 15B result for K=1 MuLoCo is acknowledged by the authors themselves to use a batch size in a 'local minimum' region rather than the true optimum (identified only after the fact), which undermines confidence in the reported Pareto-optimality and matching-baseline claims at the largest scale.

The explanation for why K=1 DiLoCo outperforms its DP baseline more than K=1 MuLoCo does (a central and somewhat counter-intuitive finding) is purely speculative ('we hypothesize...it stands to reason') with no direct experiment isolating the proposed mechanism (reduced benefit of outer momentum for already-aligned Muon steps).

The paper explicitly reports failing to reproduce a key finding from prior work (Charles et al. 2025's monotonic improvement of DiLoCo/worker-scaling with model size) and lists several plausible confounds without resolving which one is responsible, weakening confidence in the scaling-law extrapolations that are central to the paper's largest claims.

The Limitations section is truncated mid-sentence ('we did not evaluate the perfor'), and overall the limitations discussion is quite thin relative to the number of strong extrapolative claims made (dense-transformer-only, 20 TPP-only, no MoE/SSM, no repeated seeds, single hyperparameter set used per scale).

The core methodological contribution itself (swap AdamW for Muon inside DiLoCo) is a simple, low-novelty combination of two known techniques; the paper's novelty rests almost entirely on the empirical/analytical characterization of *why* it helps, and that characterization, while suggestive, stops short of a rigorous causal argument (correlational cosine-similarity and spectral analyses, not interventional).

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: over 2,200 pre-training runs across 150M-15B parameter scales, with extensive per-scale hyperparameter sweeps (inner/outer LR, weight decay, batch size, momentum) for four optimizers x five worker counts, giving strong confidence that comparisons are not artifacts of unequal tuning effort.

The central claim (MuLoCo scales better with workers than DiLoCo even after normalizing by respective DP baselines) is well supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: absolute/relative loss curves (Fig 1, 6), pseudogradient cosine-similarity analysis (Fig 2, 4), spectral collapse/interference-gap analysis (Fig 3), and a theoretical proposition (4.2) plus corollaries linking pseudogradient nuclear norm to per-step alignment and Frobenius-norm stability (Fig 5), which together provide a coherent mechanistic story rather than a purely empirical correlation.

Practically valuable and comprehensive robustness checks: results hold under long synchronization intervals (H up to 240), under quantization (2/4/8-bit, linear and statistical, with/without error feedback) and top-k sparsification, under Streaming/partitioned communication, and in measured (not just simulated) wall-clock time on real H100 clusters, showing <1% optimizer step overhead for Muon.

Demonstrates a genuinely new and practically important finding for K=1 (single-worker DiLoCo/lookahead-style setting): MuLoCo achieves a larger critical batch size than DP Muon while matching or exceeding its performance, yielding a Pareto-optimal training-time/performance tradeoff (Fig 12, 13) — a distinct and useful contribution beyond the K>1 worker-scaling story.

Validation at 15B scale (with hyperparameters extrapolated via fitted power laws rather than swept) adds credibility that the scaling trends generalize beyond the swept 150M-3.1B range, including matched zero-shot downstream benchmark performance despite much larger batch sizes.

Careful, transparent methodology in secondary details: robust smoothed evaluation-loss estimator (time-weighted EMA at sync boundaries) with explicit justification and examples (Fig 23), explicit modeling of realistic all-to-all reduce-scatter + ring all-gather for quantized communication rather than an idealized collective, and clear algorithm boxes for compressed/EF variants.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Prop 4.2 and corollaries) is a fairly generic algebraic identity relating nuclear norm to per-step cosine alignment and Frobenius norms; it does not by itself explain *why* Muon's steps are more mutually aligned across workers or why AdamW's steps have more variable Frobenius norms across workers — these remain empirical observations that the theory formalizes post hoc rather than predicts, so the causal mechanism behind MuLoCo's advantage is still not fully pinned down (the authors themselves note they "do not show a direct causal link").

The 15B experiments are not hyperparameter-swept (only extrapolated via power laws fit on smaller/no larger scales for some hyperparameters), and the paper itself flags that the K=1 MuLoCo batch size used at 15B was likely a local minimum discovered too late, meaning the flagship 15B result for K=1 MuLoCo is probably an underestimate of its true performance — this introduces some uncertainty into the headline scaling claims at the largest tested scale.

Discrepancy with prior work (Charles et al. 2025) regarding monotonic improvement of DiLoCo relative to DP with model size is acknowledged but not resolved; the authors list several plausible confounds (data, eval loss computation, outer momentum tuning, LR decay to 1/10) without disentangling which actually drives the difference, leaving open questions about robustness of the scaling-law extrapolations.

Limitations section is abruptly truncated mid-sentence ("Finally, we did not evaluate the perfor"), suggesting an editing/formatting error; while minor, this and other typos (e.g., 'accelearted', 'Netotron-CC', 'cahnges', 'chinchilla-optimial') suggest the manuscript could benefit from a careful proofreading pass before publication.

The study is restricted to dense transformers in a single ~20 TPP regime; generalization to MoE/SSM architectures, non-chinchilla-optimal token ratios, or much larger (>15B) scales is untested, which the authors appropriately flag but which still limits the immediate applicability of the strong scaling claims to the very largest frontier models mentioned in the introduction (2-15T parameters).

Some scaling-law fitting choices (e.g., choice of shared irreducible loss L_irr=1.711 fit via a 512-restart L-BFGS with Huber loss) are reported to underestimate 15B performance, and the paper acknowledges this discrepancy without a fully satisfying resolution, slightly weakening confidence in the compute-scaling exponent comparisons (α) used to argue MuLoCo scales better with compute.
